claims.text: The as-quenched equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline has a homogeneous, fully disordered, single-phase structure.
Brittle behavior in single-phase CoCrFeMnNi-based HEAs can emerge because of intragranular nanoscale chemical clusters.
Adding approximately 0.1 mol fraction Al can produce intragranular chemical clusters in the CoCrFeMnNi-based alloy.
Aging at 300–500 °C can produce short-range-order clusters in as-quenched CoCrFeMnNi.
Rapid solidification, approximately 1200 °C homogenization, and rapid quenching can retain a single-phase Al-modified alloy while inducing localized chemical clustering.
Aging for 1–100 hours at 300–500 °C can develop nanoscale short-range order without overt secondary-phase precipitation.
The relevant clusters form within grains rather than at grain boundaries.
Nanoscale chemical or short-range-order clusters impede dislocation motion.
The intragranular clusters create localized stress concentrations.
Cluster-induced dislocation impediment and stress concentration promote local crack initiation and early mechanical failure.
The proposed intragranular-clustering mechanism is distinct from grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation mechanisms associated with conventional alloys.
Both Al-modified and aged specimens will have lower toughness than the as-quenched baseline.
Both Al-modified and aged specimens will initiate cracks earlier than the as-quenched baseline.
Treated specimens will exhibit a greater tendency toward intragranular rather than grain-boundary fracture features.
Al-modified and aged specimens will contain a higher density of intragranular nanoscale clusters than the as-quenched baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate thermal exposure where extensive grain coarsening, macroscopic phase separation, and classical precipitation do not occur.
The predicted embrittlement can occur under both quasi-static and dynamic mechanical loading.
